Feral Finder

Ranger-led feral animal tracking for Lama Lama Country

An offline-first mobile app that helps the Lama Lama Rangers record, share and predict feral animal activity on Country, so limited time and budget go where they protect the most.

Try the prototypeRead the background

Acknowledgement of Country

We acknowledge the Gadigal people of the Eora Nation, Traditional Custodians of the land on which this project was developed, and pay respect to their Elders past and present. We also acknowledge the Lama Lama people, Traditional Owners of the Land and Sea Country at the centre of this work, and recognise that the knowledge guiding it belongs to them.

Executive summary

Feral Finder: Ranger-led feral animal tracking for Lama Lama Country

A phone app that lets every Ranger log feral animal sightings and baits, share one live map with the team, and see where hidden animals such as feral pigs are likely to be.

Design Area: 4 Augmenting the Ranger Program (Project Opportunity 4.3 Feral animal management)

Keywords: feral pigs, feral cattle, feral animals, Ranger program, offline mobile app, local first, predictive mapping, Indigenous data sovereignty, Cape York, Lama Lama Country

Proposal Summary

The project aims to help the Lama Lama Rangers find and manage feral animals that are hard to detect, especially feral pigs, through a Ranger-owned mobile app that records sightings and baits, shares them with the whole team, and predicts where unseen animals are likely to be. Feral Finder turns scattered field observations into structured data. For the Rangers, this means a shared, living map, so management efforts can be directed strategically. More broadly, it fills a data gap in published research and builds an evidence base for the effectiveness of Ranger work, helping make the case for continued funding.

Overview of Design

  • Feral Finder achieves Ranger-directed feral animal control through an offline-first phone app with four parts: a radar-style map, sighting and bait reports, a shared log and team chat.
  • For species that cannot be seen from the air, a habitat-likelihood model combines past sightings, water, vegetation and season to mark ‘likely’ zones, each with a confidence score that Rangers verify with a camera or patrol.
  • Implementation is supported by co-design workshops, a dry-season pilot with one Ranger team, and a data governance agreement that keeps all data with Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation (YAC).
  • The design does not rely on fixed field infrastructure. It runs on Ranger phones, syncs through the existing Starlink connection at base, and can use optional camera traps to verify predictions.

Key Considerations

  • Co-design with the Rangers and approval by YAC and Elders must come before any build.
  • A written data governance agreement should confirm that YAC owns the data and holds a licence to the app code.
  • Cultural site locations stay in a restricted layer visible only to approved Ranger accounts.
  • Predictions are prompts, not proof: every predicted zone needs field verification.
  • Logging works offline during wet-season isolation, but sharing waits until a Ranger is back in range.
  • Ongoing costs for maintenance, hosting and model review need funding beyond the pilot.

Proposed Materials and Cost Summary

Port Stewart is in Australia, so the local currency is the Australian dollar (A$).

  • Purchased materials: up to three rugged phones (only if existing phones are unsuitable), ten optional wildlife cameras, a cloud database subscription.
  • Other materials: existing Ranger phones, the Starlink connection at base, open-source mapping and AI libraries.
  • Labour: contract app developer; consulting ecologist (about 120 hours over three years); lawyer (about 20 hours); Ranger time for co-design and training (about 120 hours in Year 1).

Background

Port Stewart, known as Yintjingga, sits on the eastern Cape York Peninsula around Princess Charlotte Bay. It is part of Lama Lama Country, where the Lama Lama Rangers care for Land and Sea Country through a program run by Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation (Engineers Without Borders Australia [EWB], 2026). This project responds to Design Area 4, Augmenting the Ranger Program, and Project Opportunity 4.3, feral animal management, considering monitoring, trapping and the operational needs of the Ranger Program (EWB, 2026).

Why feral animals matter here

The Lama Lama National Park management statement records 266 plant and 120 animal species, including threatened species such as the little tern and eastern curlew (Department of Environment, Science and Innovation [DESI], 2024). It describes extensive damage to soil, plants and animals from feral pigs, with watercourse and wetland soils severely affected in the wet season, and links cattle to salt incursion and wind erosion (DESI, 2024). Across northern Australia, feral cattle, buffalo and pigs degrade soil, water quality, waterholes and vegetation, and the resulting habitat loss is the main driver of native wildlife decline (Mihailou & Massaro, 2021).

93.1%of marine turtle nest losses on western Cape York came from predation (Whytlaw et al., 2013)
89.6%of those losses were caused by feral pigs alone (Whytlaw et al., 2013)

The harm is cultural as well as ecological. Feral pigs, cattle, horses and buffalo damage traditional food and cultural resources such as turtles, water lilies and crocodile eggs (NESP Resilient Landscapes Hub, n.d.).

What is already being done

Feral cattle are mustered between August and December to remove them from protected areas while building the breeding stock of the community’s cattle enterprise, which also provides income and jobs (YAC, n.d.-b). Pig control draws on trapping and baiting (Bengsen et al., 2011; EWB, 2026). In the field, the Rangers combine knowledge passed down through Elders with tools such as iTracker, Fulcrum and limited drone use (EWB, 2026), and they monitor freshwater wetlands for the impacts of feral animals and weeds (YAC, n.d.-c).

Why this is not enough

Three gaps limit what this effort can achieve.

First, feral pigs are hard to find. They are smaller than cattle, concentrate around watercourses and wetlands (DESI, 2024), and forage in small, discrete areas, often alone or in small groups (Whytlaw et al., 2013). A mob of cattle on an open floodplain is easy to see from the air, but pigs under cover are not.

Second, there is no simple way to see whether control is working. A count of animals removed does not show whether turtle nests or wetlands were protected.

Third, the wet season isolates Port Stewart for months (EWB, 2026), so a tool that needs constant connectivity fails when it is needed most. Baiting also needs careful records, because shallow burial reduces bait uptake by most non-target species (Bengsen et al., 2011).

Problem description

Lama Lama Rangers need a way to direct feral animal control using their own field data, so that effort protects the sites that matter most on Country.

Today, sightings, bait locations and damage notes are spread across people, notebooks and general-purpose apps, and the animals causing the most damage are the least likely to be seen. In the ideal situation, every Ranger can log what they see in seconds, even with no signal; the whole team shares one up-to-date picture; likely hidden activity is flagged for checking; and YAC holds the data and decides how it is used.

Design criteria and selection

The EWB brief states that the best tools in Ranger contexts work offline and sync later, use common parts and power supplies, need minimal training and produce immediate operational value (EWB, 2026). We built six criteria on those points, adding Ranger data ownership and the core problem of finding hidden animals.

Design criteria

Works offline

All core tasks, such as viewing the map and logging a sighting or bait, work with no signal, and queued records sync with no loss or duplication.

Port Stewart is isolated in the wet season, and patrol areas have little or no coverage (EWB, 2026).

Minimal training

A new user can log a sighting in under 60 seconds after a ten-minute introduction.

The brief favours tools that need minimal training (EWB, 2026), and Ranger time is limited.

Ranger ownership

Data is stored in an account YAC controls, and nothing leaves the Ranger team without YAC approval.

Indigenous data governance means Indigenous peoples decide what data is collected and how it is used (Maiam nayri Wingara Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Data Sovereignty Collective [Maiam nayri Wingara], 2018).

Finds hidden animals

The design gives location evidence across the whole patrol area for species that aerial surveys miss, especially pigs.

Pigs cause most turtle nest losses yet are the hardest animals to see (Whytlaw et al., 2013).

Affordable to run

Yearly running costs stay below a third (33%) of the Year 1 cost.

Grants often cover set-up, so long-term costs must be low enough for YAC to sustain.

Common parts

The design runs on standard phones and power, with no components in the field that need servicing.

The brief asks for common parts and power supplies (EWB, 2026), and wet-season access prevents field repairs.

Three design options

Option 1: Smart trap network — Discarded

Remote-controlled pig traps with an AI camera that counts pigs inside and closes the gate. In NSW, the PigIT system has trapped feral pigs this way using an edge-based AI camera, solar power and a wireless gate actuator (Intersect Australia, n.d.). However, commercial remote gates depend on a mobile signal and cost about US$1,600 per controller before panels, camera and battery (Simmons Sporting Goods, n.d.), and traps only catch pigs where they stand.

Option 2: AI camera-trap network — Partially implemented

A grid of wildlife cameras whose images are sorted by open-source AI. MegaDetector finds animals, people and vehicles in camera images, and SpeciesNet classifies animals to species level (Google, n.d.). Rangers would swap memory cards on patrol and run the models on a laptop at base. This works without signal and records pigs at night, but it only covers the points where cameras stand, each camera costs about A$860 (Reconyx Australia, n.d.), and general-purpose models would need checking against local species.

Option 3: Feral Finder app — Chosen

An offline-first app in which Rangers log sightings, damage and baits in one tap, see everyone’s records on a shared map, and receive predicted ‘likely’ zones for hidden species. It builds on a proven idea: Aak Puul Ngantam rangers on western Cape York used a purpose-built survey app that gave their team immediate access to feral pig data (NESP Resilient Landscapes Hub, n.d.).

Decision matrix

Each option was scored from 1 (does not meet the criterion) to 5 (fully meets it), and each score was multiplied by the criterion’s weight.

CriterionWeightSmart trapsCamera networkFeral Finder
Works offline20%245

Affordable to run15%234

Weighted score (out of 5)2.753.604.50

Smart traps scored low on offline use and common parts because gates need a signal and field servicing. The camera network works offline and sees pigs at night but only covers fixed points. Feral Finder works across the whole patrol area with no signal or field hardware; it lost a point on finding animals because predictions need verifying, and on training because Rangers must learn the zone display.

We selected Feral Finder (4.50). The camera network scored second and remains useful: the selected design keeps optional cameras to verify predicted zones, and the Recommendations propose adding automatic image sorting later.

How Feral Finder works

Feral Finder is a phone app for individual Rangers. It is built as an offline-first web app that installs to a phone’s home screen, so it needs no app store account and runs on the Android and Apple phones Rangers already carry.

Radar map

Shows the Ranger’s position, confirmed sightings as red dots, predicted zones as yellow circles and baits as blue diamonds. It filters by species, and predictions can be switched off.

Reports

Logs a sighting (species, number, photo and damage to wetlands, soil, fences or cultural sites) or a bait (type, number, date). GPS is captured automatically.

Shared log

Lists every Ranger’s reports in one place, filtered by sightings or baits, with each record’s sync status. Each record also helps the prediction model improve.

Team chat

Lets the field team coordinate, with sighting and bait cards attached to messages.

How data moves

Reports are saved on the phone first. When a Ranger returns to base, the app syncs through the existing connection to a database in an account owned by YAC and hosted in Australia. The prediction model runs on that database and sends updated zones back to every phone at the next sync, so the latest zones are available offline on patrol.

How the prediction works

For species that cannot be seen from the air, Feral Finder predicts where they are likely to be instead of trying to spot them. The model combines three inputs:

  • Confirmed sightings from Rangers and cameras
  • Environmental layers such as distance to water, vegetation and season
  • Known animal behaviour, such as pigs foraging repeatedly in small, discrete areas (Whytlaw et al., 2013) and concentrating on wetland soils in the wet season (DESI, 2024)
The output is a ‘likely’ zone with a confidence score. A consulting ecologist designs and checks the model with the Rangers, and it is kept simple enough that each zone can explain itself, for example ‘near permanent water, three sightings in two weeks’.

Predictions are prompts, not sightings. A zone says where a camera, bait or patrol is worth placing; it never says an animal is definitely there.

Community concerns and how the design responds

Table 2. Likely community concerns and design responses.
ConcernResponse
Will outsiders see sensitive places?Cultural site locations sit in a restricted layer visible only to approved Ranger accounts, and YAC controls all sharing (Maiam nayri Wingara, 2018).
Will the AI tell us what to do?The app only suggests, and Rangers decide. Each zone shows its reasons and confidence.
Is this extra work?An easy logging system replaces notebook entries, and syncing happens automatically.
What about the cattle enterprise?Cattle sightings help plan the August to December muster, which removes feral cattle while building breeding stock (YAC, n.d.-b).
What if there is no signal?Everything works offline; sharing waits until the Ranger is back at base.
What if baits harm other animals?Bait records include method and any non-target observations, supporting safer baiting (Bengsen et al., 2011).

Research on feral buffalo in northern Australia shows that pest management works best when it respects that Traditional Owners may value an animal as both a problem and a resource (Robinson & Whitehead, 2003; Albrecht et al., 2009). Feral Finder supports that balance by recording information without deciding what should happen to an animal.

Prototype and testing

Figure 4 is the working prototype. Drag the map, tap the markers, and try Report, Log and Chat. All data is illustrative.

Figure 4. Feral Finder interactive prototype. Built by Team Rangers.

What was prototyped and why

We prototyped the Ranger-facing app because its riskiest assumptions are about people rather than hardware: that a Ranger can log a sighting quickly in the field, that users can tell a confirmed sighting from a prediction, and that the offline and sync behaviour is easy to understand. The prediction model itself was not built; the prototype shows example zones so their presentation could be tested.

How it was built

It is a web app built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript that runs in any phone browser and installs to the home screen.

How the design changed

Table 3. Prototype iterations and the feedback that drove them.
VersionFeedbackChange made
v1 Radar conceptPredicted zones looked stretched into ovals, suggesting a direction the data does not have; markers crowded together.Zones redrawn as true circles inside the map; markers spaced apart.
v2 Individual RangerThe map centred on a ‘Ranger Base’, but the app is for individual Rangers; baiting, a core practice, was missing.Map centred on ‘You’; bait reports and bait markers added; shared log tab added.
v3 Usable mapThe fixed map could not be explored. Final presentation feedback asked for testing results.Pannable, zoomable map with a recentre button; offline sync status shown; full-screen install mode; usability test run.

How it was tested

Five participants each received a 30-second introduction, then completed five tasks on a phone while one of us timed them and noted errors. Participants were university students acting as proxies, as Rangers could not be reached within the project (see Recommendations).

Table 4. Usability test tasks and success targets.
TaskWhat it testsTarget
T1 Log a feral pig sightingSpeed of field loggingUnder 60 seconds
T2 Say which markers are confirmed and which are predictedUnderstanding of AI zonesAll participants correct
T3 Find the bait set by Wilfred and say how many baitsMap and bait recordsUnder 30 seconds
T4 Explain what ‘Offline, 3 pending’ meansUnderstanding of syncCorrect explanation
T5 Show only pig records on the mapFiltersUnder 15 seconds

Results

Table 5. Usability test results. Full data in Appendix 3.
TaskSuccessMedian timeNotes
T15/515.32 sParticipants initially tapped on the "Log" tab instead of "Report". This is likely due to our phrasing of the task, and not an issue with the app.
T25/5N/ANo issues at all. Participants were able to identify this very easily.
T35/516.44 sParticipants were able to complete this task, but most of them searched for the specific bait from the radar instead of just checking the log, which would make it much more efficient.
T43/5N/AParticipants knew what "offline" meant, but they couldn't reliably explain the details of syncing offline data.
T55/51.45 sParticipants were easily able to filter the radar to show only pigs.
What testing confirmed
The app's core functions proved efficient and intuitive for new users, meeting the targets for four of the five tasks. All five participants succeeded at Tasks 1, 2, 3 and 5, easily identifying AI zones and using map filters, and median times were well below the limits: logging a sighting took roughly 15 seconds against a 60-second target, and filtering the map took just 1.5 seconds against a 15-second target.
What needs improving
The sync status needs clearer communication: Task 4 was the only task that missed its target, with only three of five participants able to explain it. Users understood being offline, but not how offline data syncs. The workflow could also guide users toward better habits, as in Task 3 participants searched the radar for a bait instead of using the more efficient log view. Some participants tapped "Log" instead of "Report" in Task 1, though this was attributed to the prompt's phrasing rather than the app's design. Finally, testing relied on university students rather than Rangers, which future testing must address to ensure field accuracy.

Implementation plan

Feral Finder is introduced in four phases over about twelve months, timed around the seasons. Consultation and building happen during the wet season, when travel is limited, and the field pilot runs in the dry season, when the Rangers can reach Country (EWB, 2026).

Phase 1: Consult and agree (months 1–3)

YAC, the Rangers and Elders review the concept. Co-design workshops shape the screens and species list, a data governance agreement confirms YAC ownership of the data and code licence, and rules are set for the restricted cultural layer.

Phase 2: Build (months 2–6)

A contract developer builds the app and database. The ecologist designs the model using existing Lama Lama records, and two Rangers test early versions.

Phase 3: Dry-season pilot (months 5–9)

One Ranger team uses Feral Finder alongside current methods. Training is one day on Country using a train-the-trainer model: the two already-trained Rangers support others, with a laminated quick guide for the field. Ten optional cameras verify predicted zones.

Phase 4: Review and expand (months 9–12)

We review the evaluation results with YAC, fix issues and extend the app to all Rangers. Cattle sightings support planning for the August to December muster (YAC, n.d.-b).

Maintenance and repair

There is no field infrastructure to maintain. If a phone breaks, the Ranger signs in on another device and nothing is lost, because records are stored on the server after each sync with daily backups (Supabase, n.d.). If the app fails, Rangers return to paper notes and enter them later. A developer support arrangement covers updates and bug fixes, and the ecologist reviews the model once a year before the dry season.

Ownership

YAC owns the database account, the data and a licence to the app code, so it can change developers without losing anything. Following Indigenous data governance principles, YAC decides what is collected, who can see it and whether researchers or government can use it (Maiam nayri Wingara, 2018). Over time, the Rangers take over training, and Junior Rangers can learn the app.

User journey map

The map follows one Ranger through a patrol day. The design targets its lowest points today: no signal at a sighting, lost track of bait sites and not knowing whether effort helped.

Funding the project

Two Queensland programs fit directly. The Queensland Indigenous Land and Sea Ranger Program funds First Nations organisations to employ rangers (Funding Centre, n.d.), and in 2025 the Queensland Government committed funding through the Queensland Feral Pest Initiative to develop new feral pig control methods over three years (“Queensland Government Boosts Feral Pig Funding,” 2025). Feral Finder also strengthens future applications: Aak Puul Ngantam used data from its survey app to report straightforwardly to funders, including the Queensland Land and Sea Ranger program (NESP Resilient Landscapes Hub, n.d.).

What it is worth

Feral Finder does not earn income, so its value lies in better use of existing budgets. When Aak Puul Ngantam used its data to focus a limited aerial control budget on turtle nesting coast, it maintained a 90% reduction in predation of three threatened turtle species along 48 km of beach (NESP Resilient Landscapes Hub, n.d.). Feral Finder also tracks Ranger hours per verified detection, giving YAC cost evidence that does not exist today.

Table 9. Risk register.
RiskLikelihoodImpactMitigation

Environmental: The design adds no structures to Country. Its footprint is limited to phones and optional cameras, which should be repaired where possible and recycled through e-waste programs at end of life.

Legal: Poison baits are regulated products, so accurate bait records also support record-keeping obligations. The lawyer should review privacy settings in Phase 1.

Social: Feral Finder builds digital skills for Rangers and Junior Rangers and gives YAC evidence of the value of Ranger work.

Recommendations

  1. Consult before building. Present this proposal to YAC, the Rangers and Elders, and proceed only with their approval and changes.
  2. Sign a data governance agreement early, covering ownership, access, the restricted layer and research use.
  3. Test with Rangers on Country. Repeat the usability test with Rangers, because student participants cannot reflect field conditions.
  4. Partner with researchers to validate the model, as CSIRO and NESP researchers did with Aak Puul Ngantam (NESP Resilient Landscapes Hub, n.d.).
  5. Add automatic camera image sorting in a second stage using open-source models (Google, n.d.), combining the strengths of Option 2.
  6. Check exports to iTracker and Fulcrum, then extend the app to related work such as weed mapping under Project Opportunity 4.1 (EWB, 2026).
  7. Secure multi-year funding for running costs before the pilot ends.

Appendix 4: Use of generative AI and prompt log

Generative AI tools were used as a technical and editorial assistant to support the presentation and verification of our work, while all research, engineering design decisions, cost benchmarking, and usability testing were conducted by us. Specifically, AI was used to overcome the layout limitations of Google Sites by converting our drafted report pages (exported as PDFs) and project graphics into a self-contained HTML/CSS code embed, building the interactive phone prototype which we really wanted to include, verifying our multi-year budget calculations, and summarizing our raw usability test observations. All AI-generated code, calculations, and text were manually reviewed, tested, and edited by the team for accuracy.
